q: what is the world wide web
a: The Internet is a global network of interconnected computers that communicate using standard protocols (TCP/IP). The World Wide Web (WWW) is an information system on the Internet that allows documents to be connected via hyperlinks and accessed through web browsers.

A computer is an electronic device that processes data by executing instructions. The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is the 'brain' that performs calculations by running a fetch-decode-execute cycle billions of times per second. It works with RAM (memory), storage (SSD/hard drive), and input/output devices.

A computer works by executing instructions stored in memory. The CPU fetches instructions from RAM, decodes them, performs the requested operation (arithmetic, logic, data movement), and stores results. This fetch-decode-execute cycle repeats billions of times per second, coordinated by a clock signal.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is the simulation of human intelligence in machines. It includes machine learning (training models on data), natural language processing, computer vision, and reasoning systems. AI can be narrow (designed for specific tasks) or general (theoretical human-level intelligence across domains).

q: what is the difference between ram and storage
a: RAM (Random Access Memory) is fast, temporary memory that the computer uses to store data currently being worked on. It is volatile — contents are lost when power is off. Storage (SSD, hard drive) is slower but permanent — it retains data when the computer is off. Think of RAM as your desk and storage as filing cabinets.

Wi-Fi uses radio waves (typically 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz bands) to transmit data between devices and a router. The router connects to the internet via a modem and converts data into radio signals. Devices with Wi-Fi receivers decode these signals. Wi-Fi standards (802.11ax, etc.) define speed and frequency.

q: how many programming languages are there
a: A programming language is a formal language with instructions that a computer can execute. There are hundreds of programming languages, each designed for different purposes. Major ones include Python (general-purpose), JavaScript (web), C/C++ (systems), Java (enterprise), Rust (systems/safe), and Go (cloud/network).

An algorithm is a step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem or completing a task. Like a recipe, it takes inputs, follows defined steps, and produces outputs. Sorting, searching, and compression are common algorithm categories. Efficiency is measured in time complexity (how fast) and space complexity (memory used).

Moore's Law is the observation by Gordon Moore (co-founder of Intel) in 1965 that the number of transistors on a microchip doubles approximately every two years, while the cost halves. This trend held for decades, driving exponential growth in computing power, though it has slowed in recent years due to physical limits.
